summary: Specifies the Mapping of Address and Port using Translation architecture. It uses stateless IPv6-IPv4 NAT64 translation to give IPv4 connectivity across an IPv6 network with shared or non-shared IPv4 addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: MAP-T lets a network that runs on IPv6 still serve users whose devices only speak IPv4. Each customer router translates between the two protocols and, when IPv4 addresses are scarce, several customers share one IPv4 address. Because the translation is computed from rules rather than remembered, no state has to be kept in the network for each connection.

subtitle: How an IPv6-only network can carry IPv4 users, with shared addresses, using stateless translation instead of tunnels.

tldr.problem: Public IPv4 addresses are running out, so a network that has moved to IPv6 still has to serve IPv4 users. Those users may have to share one IPv4 address, which means the IPv4 address and the port range have to be derived from the IPv6 address without keeping any state.
tldr.mechanism: MAP-T combines a stateful NAPT44 function at the customer edge with a stateless NAT64 function. A set of rules, shared by every device in a MAP domain, says how an IPv4 address, a port set and an IPv6 address are computed from one another.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 users keep their service across an IPv6-only network, with addresses shared by the configured ratio, and no per-flow state in the network. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Interface identifier
facts.value: 16 bits of zero, 32-bit IPv4 address, 16-bit PSID

today: RFC 7599 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2015, and it has not been obsoleted. It is the translation-based member of the MAP family; the encapsulation-based member is RFC 7597 (MAP-E), and the two share the same mapping rules.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Experience from early service provider IPv6 deployments, such as the one described in RFC 6219, indicates that a successful transition to IPv6 can happen while legacy IPv4 users are still supported, without a full end-to-end dual-IP-stack deployment. Because of public IPv4 address exhaustion, this requires an IPv6 technology that supports IPv4 users on shared IPv4 addressing, while letting the operator keep working to IPv6 network practices.

Using double NAT64 translation-based solutions is an effective way to meet these requirements, especially combined with stateless translation techniques that reduce the operational burden described in the 4v6 solutions work.

The Mapping of Address and Port using Translation (MAP-T) architecture specified here is such a double stateless NAT64-based solution. It builds on the stateless NAT64 techniques of RFC 6145 and on the stateless algorithmic address and transport-layer port-mapping scheme defined for MAP-E in RFC 7597. MAP-T differs from MAP-E in using IPv4-IPv6 translation rather than encapsulation as the form of IPv6 domain transport. Translation is advantageous where encapsulation overhead rules out encapsulation, or where IPv6 operational practices such as the use of IPv6-only servers, or reliance on IPv6 plus protocol headers for traffic classification, make encapsulation unsuitable.
sections.plainLanguage: MAP-E carries IPv4 traffic across an IPv6 network by wrapping each packet in an outer IPv6 packet. MAP-T instead converts the packet from IPv4 to IPv6 and back, so the IPv6 network sees ordinary IPv6 traffic and there is no extra header to carry.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
A MAP Customer Edge (CE) is a device functioning as a customer edge router in a MAP deployment. A typical MAP CE adopting MAP Rules serves a residential site with one WAN-side IPv6-addressed interface and one or more LAN-side interfaces addressed using private IPv4 addressing.

A MAP Border Relay (BR) is a MAP-enabled router managed by the service provider at the edge of a MAP domain. It has at least an IPv6-enabled interface and an IPv4 interface connected to the native IPv4 network.

A MAP domain is one or more MAP CEs and BRs connected by an IPv6 network and sharing a common set of MAP Rules. A service provider may deploy a single MAP domain or may use multiple MAP domains.

A MAP Rule is a set of parameters describing the mapping between an IPv4 prefix, IPv4 address or shared IPv4 address and an IPv6 prefix or address. Each MAP domain uses a different mapping rule set. A MAP rule set is composed of all the MAP Rules communicated to a device that are meant to determine its IP and port mapping and forwarding operations, and is also called a MAP rule table or simply a rule table. Two specific types of rule, the Basic Mapping Rule (BMR) and the Forwarding Mapping Rule (FMR), are defined in Section 5 of RFC 7597. The Default Mapping Rule (DMR) is defined in this document.

Each node has a separate part of the transport-layer port space, which is called a port set. A Port Set ID (PSID) algorithmically identifies a set of ports exclusively assigned to a CE. A shared IPv4 address is an IPv4 address shared among multiple CEs, where only ports belonging to the assigned port set may be used for communication; it is also known as a port-restricted IPv4 address.

The End-user IPv6 prefix is the IPv6 prefix assigned to an end-user CE by means other than MAP itself, for example through DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation, Stateless Address Autoconfiguration or manual configuration, and it is unique for each CE. The MAP IPv6 address is the IPv6 address used to reach the MAP function of a CE from other CEs and from BRs. The Rule IPv6 prefix and the Rule IPv4 prefix are the IPv6 and IPv4 prefixes assigned by a service provider for a MAP Rule. The Embedded Address (EA) bits in the IPv6 address identify an IPv4 prefix or address, or part of one, or a shared IPv4 address or part of one, together with a Port Set Identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The main pieces are the customer router, the CE, the provider's border router, the BR, and the set of rules they share. A rule says how an IPv4 address, a range of port numbers and an IPv6 address are related, so that any device in the domain can compute the same answer without asking anyone.

sections.title: Architecture
sections.content:
The MAP-T architecture connects any number of privately addressed IPv4 users, N and M, by means of MAP-T CEs to an IPv6 network equipped with one or more MAP-T BRs. CEs and BRs that share MAP configuration parameters, the MAP Rules, form a MAP-T domain.

Functionally, the CE and BR use and extend well-established building blocks. A NAT44 function, which is Network Address and Port Translation, on a MAP CE is extended with support for restricting the allowable TCP and UDP ports for a given IPv4 address; the IPv4 address and port range used are determined by the MAP provisioning process and are identical to MAP-E. A stateless NAT64 function is extended to allow stateless mapping of IPv4 and transport-layer port ranges to the IPv6 address space.

Each MAP-T CE is assigned a regular IPv6 prefix from the operator's IPv6 network. Together with the MAP domain configuration settings and the MAP procedures, this allows the computation of a MAP IPv6 address and a corresponding IPv4 address. To allow IPv4 address sharing, the CE may also have to be configured with a TCP and UDP port range identified by a MAP Port Set Identifier value. Each CE is responsible for forwarding traffic between a given user's private IPv4 address space and the MAP domain's IPv6 address space, using stateless NAT64 together with the MAP address computation algorithm. The MAP-T BR connects one or more MAP-T domains to external IPv4 networks using stateless NAT64 as extended by MAP-T behavior.

Unlike MAP-E, NAT64 technology is used for two purposes. First, it is intended to diminish encapsulation overhead and allow IPv4 and IPv6 traffic to be treated as similarly as possible. Second, it is intended to allow IPv4-only nodes to correspond directly with IPv6 nodes in the MAP-T domain that have IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses as per RFC 6052.

The architecture rests on three key properties: algorithmic IPv4-IPv6 address mapping codified as MAP Rules; a MAP IPv6 address identifier; and MAP-T IPv4-IPv6 forwarding behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Each customer router runs two translation functions. One is the familiar port translation that gives each device a port number of its own. The other converts IPv4 to IPv6 and back, using the shared rules. Because the rules are the same everywhere, the border router can undo the translation without keeping a list of active connections.

sections.title: Mapping Rules and the Default Mapping Rule
sections.content:
The MAP-T algorithmic mapping rules are identical to those in Section 5 of the MAP-E specification, with one exception: the forwarding of traffic to and from IPv4 destinations outside a MAP-T domain is performed as described in this document rather than as in Section 5.4 of the MAP-E specification.

IPv4 traffic sent by MAP nodes that are all within one MAP domain is translated to IPv6, with the sender's MAP IPv6 address, derived via the Basic Mapping Rule, as the IPv6 source address and the recipient's MAP IPv6 address, derived via the Forwarding Mapping Rule, as the IPv6 destination address.

IPv4-addressed destinations outside the MAP domain are represented by IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses as per RFC 6052, using the BR's IPv6 prefix. For a CE sending traffic to such a destination, the source address of the IPv6 packet is the CE's MAP IPv6 address and the destination IPv6 address is the destination IPv4-embedded IPv6 address. This address mapping is said to follow the MAP-T Default Mapping Rule, and it is defined in terms of the IPv6 prefix advertised by one or more BRs that provide external connectivity. A typical MAP-T CE installs an IPv4 default route using this rule, and a BR uses it when translating all outside IPv4 source addresses to the IPv6 MAP domain.

The DMR IPv6 prefix length should be 64 bits long by default and in any case must not exceed 96 bits. The mapping of the IPv4 destination behind the IPv6 prefix follows the /64 rule of RFC 6052 by default, and any trailing bits after the IPv4 address are set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of rule work together. The basic rule says which IPv4 address and port range this customer gets. The forwarding rules say which IPv4 destinations inside the domain are translated as a domain address. The default rule covers every other IPv4 destination on the Internet, using the border router's own prefix.

sections.title: The IPv6 Interface Identifier
sections.content:
The interface identifier format of a MAP-T node is the same as the format described in Section 6 of RFC 7597, and is repeated here for convenience. The 64 bits after the 128-n-o-s bits are laid out as 16 bits of zero, then a 32-bit IPv4 address, then a 16-bit Port Set ID.

In the case of an IPv4 prefix, the IPv4 address field is right-padded with zeros up to 32 bits. The PSID is left-padded with zeros to create a 16-bit field. For an IPv4 prefix or a complete IPv4 address, the PSID field is zero. If the End-user IPv6 prefix length is larger than 64, the most significant parts of the interface identifier are overwritten by the prefix.

Appendix A of the document works through the arithmetic. With an end-user IPv6 prefix of 2001:db8:0012:3400::/56 and a basic mapping rule of 2001:db8:0000::/40, 192.0.2.0/24 and an EA-bit length of 16, the PSID length is 8, giving a sharing ratio of 256. The IPv4 address 192.0.2.18 with PSID 0x34 gives the MAP IPv6 address 2001:db8:0012:3400:0000:c000:0212:0034, and the CE may then use 63 port ranges, from 1232-1235 through 64720-64723.
sections.plainLanguage: The last 64 bits of a MAP-T IPv6 address carry the customer information. Sixteen bits are zero, the next 32 hold the IPv4 address, and the last 16 hold the identifier of the port set. Any device that knows the rule can read the IPv4 address and the port set straight out of the IPv6 address.

sections.title: Packet Forwarding
sections.content:
IPv4 to IPv6 at the CE. A MAP-T CE receiving IPv4 packets should perform NAPT44 processing and create any necessary NAPT44 bindings. The source address and source port range of the resulting packets must correspond to the source IPv4 address and source transport port range assigned to the CE by the Basic Mapping Rule. The IPv4 packet is then subject to a longest IPv4 destination address and port match MAP Rule selection, which determines the parameters for the NAT64 operation. By default all traffic is matched to the DMR and is subject to the stateless NAT64 operation using the DMR parameters. Packets matched to optional Forwarding Mapping Rules are subject to the stateless NAT64 operation using the FMR parameters. In all cases the CE's MAP IPv6 address is used as the source address. A MAP-T CE must support a Default Mapping Rule and should support one or more Forwarding Mapping Rules.

IPv6 to IPv4 at the CE. A MAP-T CE receiving an IPv6 packet performs its regular IPv6 operations, and only packets addressed to the CE's MAP-T IPv6 addresses with source addresses matching the IPv6 MAP Rule prefixes of a DMR or FMR are processed by MAP-T, with the DMR or FMR selected on a longest match. The CE must check that each packet's transport-layer destination port number is in the range allowed by the CE's BMR configuration, and must silently drop any nonconforming packet while incrementing a counter. When a packet's source address longest matches an FMR prefix, the CE must check the source address for consistency with the allowed values derived from the allocated source port range, and if the source port is outside that range it must drop the packet and should reply with an ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable, source address failed ingress or egress policy, Type 1 Code 5. For each processed packet the CE's NAT64 function must compute an IPv4 source and destination address, the destination by extracting information from the IPv6 destination together with the BMR, and the source by classifying the packet's source against the DMR or FMR rule prefix. The resulting IPv4 packet is forwarded to the CE's NAPT44 function, where the destination IPv4 address and port number must be mapped to their original value before being forwarded by the CE's regular IPv4 rules. When NAPT44 is not enabled, the traffic from the stateless NAT64 function is forwarded directly by the CE's IPv4 rules.

IPv6 to IPv4 at the BR. A MAP-T BR receiving an IPv6 packet must select a matching MAP Rule by longest address match of the packet's source address against the MAP Rules present on the BR. Together with the Port Set ID derived from the packet's source IPv6 address, the selected rule lets the BR verify that the CE is using its allowed address and port range, so the BR must validate the consistency of the source against the allowed values from the identified port range. If the source port is outside the allowed range the BR must drop the packet and increment a counter, and should reply with the same ICMPv6 Type 1 Code 5 message. When constructing the IPv4 packet the BR must derive the source and destination IPv4 addresses and translate the IPv6-to-IPv4 headers as per RFC 6145, and the resulting packet is passed to regular IPv4 forwarding.

IPv4 to IPv6 at the BR. A MAP-T BR receiving IPv4 packets uses a longest match IPv4 and transport-layer port lookup to identify the target MAP-T domain and select the FMR and DMR rules. The BR must compute and apply the IPv6 destination addresses from the IPv4 destination address and port as per the selected FMR, and compute and apply the IPv6 source addresses from the IPv4 source address as per Section 5.1, forming an IPv6-embedded IPv4 address from the IPv4 source and the BR's IPv6 prefix. The generic IPv4-to-IPv6 header translation procedures of RFC 6145 apply throughout, and the resulting packets are passed to regular IPv6 forwarding. The operation of a BR forwarding to or from MAP-T domains defined without IPv4 address sharing is the same as that of stateless NAT64 translation.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic out of the customer site is translated at the CE and translated back at the BR. Traffic coming in is translated at the BR and translated back at the CE. At each step the device checks that the port number in the packet is one the customer is allowed to use, and drops the packet if it is not, because that is what stops one customer from reaching another's connections.

sections.title: ICMP, Fragmentation and Path MTU Discovery
sections.content:
MAP-T CEs and BRs must follow ICMP and ICMPv6 translation as per RFC 6145, but additional behavior is needed because of the NAPT44 function. Unlike TCP and UDP, which have two port fields for source and destination, the ICMP and ICMPv6 Query message header has only one ID field, which has to be used to identify the sending IPv4 host. When receiving IPv4 ICMP messages the MAP-T CE must rewrite the ID field to a port value derived from the CE's Port Set ID. A MAP-T BR receiving an IPv4 ICMP packet whose ID is bound for a shared address in the MAP-T domain should use the ID value as a substitute for the destination port in determining the IPv6 destination address, and in all other cases must derive the destination IPv6 address by simply mapping the destination IPv4 address without additional port information.

Because the IPv4 and IPv6 headers have different sizes, handling the maximum packet size matters for any system joining the two address families. There are three mechanisms: Path MTU Discovery, fragmentation, and transport-layer negotiation such as the TCP Maximum Segment Size option. MAP can use all three. The NAT64 mechanism is not lossless, so when IPv4-originated communication traverses a double NAT64 function, IPv4-originated ICMP-independent Path MTU Discovery ceases to be entirely reliable, because the DF=1 and MF=1 combination of RFC 4821 results in DF=0 and MF=1 after a double NAT64 translation.

Translating an IPv4 packet to carry it across the MAP domain increases its size, typically by 20 bytes. The MTU in the MAP domain should be well managed, and the IPv6 MTU on the CE WAN-side interface should be configured so that no fragmentation occurs within the boundary of the MAP domain. Fragmentation in MAP-T domains should be handled as described in Sections 4 and 5 of RFC 6145.

Forwarding an IPv4 packet received from outside the MAP domain needs the IPv4 destination address and the transport-protocol destination port, and the transport information is only available in the first fragment. A MAP node receiving a fragmented IPv4 packet from outside should therefore reassemble the packet before sending it into the MAP domain, though it can optimize this with a cache if the first packet received contains the transport information. In the other direction, two IPv4 hosts behind two different MAP CEs with the same IPv4 address may send fragments to an outside host using the same IPv4 fragmentation identifier, causing incorrect reassembly. Since the fragmentation identifier is a 16-bit field, it can be used in the same way as a port range, and a MAP CE should rewrite it to a value equivalent to a port of its allocated port set.

The NAT44 implemented in the MAP CE should conform to the behaviour and best current practices of RFC 4787, RFC 5508 and RFC 5382. In MAP address-sharing mode, the operation of the NAT44 must be restricted to the available port numbers derived via the Basic Mapping Rule.
sections.plainLanguage: Two details need care. ICMP messages carry one identifier rather than a port pair, so the CE rewrites that identifier to a value taken from its port set. And IPv4 fragments carry a 16-bit identifier, which two customers sharing an address could pick alike, so the CE rewrites that too, using its port set in the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Spoofing attacks. With the consistency checks between IPv4 and IPv6 sources performed on packets received by MAP nodes, MAP does not introduce any new opportunity for spoofing attacks that would not already exist in IPv6.

Denial-of-service attacks. In MAP domains where IPv4 addresses are shared, the fact that IPv4 datagram reassembly may be necessary introduces an opportunity for DoS attacks. This is inherent in address sharing and is common with other address-sharing approaches such as Dual-Stack Lite and NAT64 with DNS64. The best protection against such attacks is to accelerate IPv6 support in both clients and servers.

Routing loop attacks. Routing loop attacks may exist in some automatic tunneling scenarios and are documented in RFC 6324. They cannot exist with MAP, because each BR checks that the IPv6 source address of a received IPv6 packet is a CE address based on the Forwarding Mapping Rule.

Attacks facilitated by a restricted port set. From hosts that are not subject to ingress filtering, an attacker can inject spoofed packets during ongoing transport connections. The attacks depend on guessing which ports are currently used by target hosts. Using an unrestricted port set is preferable, that is, using native IPv6 connections that are not subject to MAP port-range restrictions. To minimize these attacks when a restricted port set is used, the MAP CE's NAT44 filtering behaviour should be Address-Dependent Filtering as described in Section 5 of RFC 4787. The MAP CEs should also use a DNS transport proxy function to handle DNS traffic, sourcing such traffic from IPv6 interfaces not assigned to MAP-T.

ICMP flooding. Given the necessity to process and translate ICMP and ICMPv6 messages at the BR and CE nodes, a foreseeable attack vector is a flood of such messages leading to saturation of the node's ICMP computing resources. This vector is not specific to MAP, and its mitigation lies in a combination of policing the rate of ICMP messages, policing the rate at which they can be processed by the MAP nodes, and identifying and blocking the sources of the traffic.

RFC 6269 outlines the general issues with IPv4 address sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: The checks that a node makes on the source address and port of incoming packets are what keep one customer from reaching another's traffic, and they also rule out routing loops. The main weakness of shared addresses is that a device may have to reassemble fragmented packets, which gives an attacker somewhere to aim a flood of traffic.
